skill.name: javascript-sdk
skill.description: JavaScript and TypeScript guidance for building inference.sh apps with @inferencesh/sdk, including agents, streaming, files, and server proxies.
skill.summary: Build inference.sh applications with the JavaScript and TypeScript SDK.
skill.author: inference-sh-9

security_audit.summary: Most static findings are false positives from Markdown examples, JavaScript template literals, placeholder URLs, and documented SDK configuration. I confirmed the eval-based tool handler examples as real high-risk patterns because agent tool input can reach dynamic code execution. I also found overbroad Bash permissions in the skill metadata, which should be narrowed before publication.

remediation.issue: Unsafe calculator examples use eval on agent tool arguments.
remediation.suggestion: Replace eval with a constrained expression parser, explicit arithmetic operations, or a vetted sandbox with strict input validation.

remediation.issue: Skill metadata allows broad npm, npx, node, pnpm, and yarn commands.
remediation.suggestion: Remove allowed-tools for a documentation-only skill or restrict commands to the smallest exact install commands needed.

remediation.issue: Some examples mention frontend public API-key configuration.
remediation.suggestion: Make backend proxy usage the only browser pattern and label direct API-key examples as server-side only.

semantic_findings.title: Overbroad Command Permissions in Skill Metadata
semantic_findings.description: The skill front matter grants Bash access for npm, npx, node, pnpm, and yarn commands. A documentation skill does not need broad Node and package-manager execution permissions, and npx can run remote package code.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The allowed-tools line directly grants broad command patterns. This is a real permission-surface risk even though the surrounding content is mainly documentation.

high_findings.description: The skill front matter grants Bash access for npm, npx, node, pnpm, and yarn commands. A documentation skill does not need broad Node and package-manager execution permissions, and npx can run remote package code.
high_findings.confidence_reasoning: The allowed-tools line directly grants broad command patterns. This is a real permission-surface risk even though the surrounding content is mainly documentation.

content.user_title: Build JavaScript AI Apps with inference.sh
content.value_statement: JavaScript teams need clear patterns for calling inference.sh from apps and services. This skill provides SDK setup, app execution, streaming, file, agent, and proxy guidance.
actual_capabilities: Install and initialize @inferencesh/sdk for Node.js, browser, React, and Next.js projects.
Run inference.sh apps with typed inputs, async tasks, sessions, and streaming progress.
Upload files from paths, buffers, browser files, URLs, and data URLs.
Create agents with tools, skills, approval flows, and model-backed app tools.
Set up backend proxy routes for Next.js, Express, Hono, Remix, and SvelteKit.
limitations: It does not provide API credentials or manage inference.sh billing.
Examples may need updates for current SDK versions and app references.
Browser apps still need a backend proxy to protect API keys.
Unsafe demo patterns, such as eval, must be replaced before production use.

best_practices: Keep API keys on the server and route browser traffic through a backend proxy.
Validate every agent tool argument and replace eval with a constrained parser or explicit operations.
Pin app references, handle task failures, and test streaming behavior before release.
anti_patterns: Do not place secret API keys in public frontend environment variables.
Do not copy eval-based calculator examples into production tools.
Do not allow agents to call external services without approval and audit logging.
